text: PepsiCo, Inc. is a leading global beverage and convenient food company that was incorporated in Delaware in 1919 and reincorporated in North Carolina in 1986. The company operates through seven reportable segments: Frito-Lay North America (FLNA), Quaker Foods North America (QFNA), PepsiCo Beverages North America (PBNA), Latin America (LatAm), Europe, Africa, Middle East and South Asia (AMESA), and Asia Pacific, Australia and New Zealand and China Region (APAC). FLNA produces and sells branded convenient foods such as Lay’s, Doritos, Cheetos, Ruffles, and Tostitos, distributed through independent distributors and retailers, and also operates a joint venture with Strauss Group to market Sabra refrigerated dips and spreads. QFNA produces and sells cereals, rice, pasta, and other branded foods like Cap’n Crunch, Life cereal, Quaker grits, and Quaker oatmeal, sold to independent distributors and retailers. PBNA manufactures and markets beverage concentrates, fountain syrups, and finished goods under brands such as Aquafina, Diet Mountain Dew, Gatorade, Pepsi, and Propel, operating its own bottling and distribution facilities and selling to authorized and independent bottlers. PBNA also produces ready-to-drink tea and coffee through joint ventures with Unilever (Lipton) and Starbucks, and manufactures licensed brands from Keurig Dr Pepper (Crush, Dr Pepper, Schweppes) and Dole Food Company and Ocean Spray Cranberries. In 2022, PBNA began distributing Hard MTN Dew, an alcoholic beverage owned by Boston Beer Company, and sold its Tropicana, Naked, and other juice brands to PAI Partners while retaining a 39% noncontrolling interest in Tropicana Brands Group (TBG), which operates across North America and Europe, with PepsiCo acting as the exclusive distributor for TBG’s portfolio in the U.S. for small-format and foodservice customers via chilled direct-store-delivery. LatAm markets and sells convenient food brands including Cheetos, Doritos, Lay’s, Ruffles, Sabritas, and Tostitos, as well as Quaker-branded products, and beverage brands such as 7UP, Diet 7UP, Gatorade, Pepsi, and Pepsi Black, sold to authorized and independent bottlers and retailers, and also distributes ready-to-drink tea through a joint venture with Unilever. Europe markets and sells convenient food brands such as Cheetos, Doritos, Lay’s, Ruffles, and Walkers, and Quaker-branded products, and beverage brands including 7UP, Diet Pepsi, Mirinda, Pepsi, and Pepsi Max, sold to authorized and independent bottlers and retailers, with some markets featuring in-house bottling and distribution, and also distributes SodaStream sparkling water makers and dairy products such as Agusha, Chudo, and Domik v Derevne, and ready-to-drink tea via a joint venture with Unilever. AMESA markets and sells convenient food brands such as Chipsy, Doritos, Kurkure, Lay’s, Sasko, Spekko, and White Star, and Quaker-branded products, and beverage brands including 7UP, Aquafina, Mirinda, Mountain Dew, and Pepsi, sold to authorized and independent bottlers and retailers, with some markets featuring in-house operations, and also distributes ready-to-drink tea through a joint venture with Unilever. The company serves customers and consumers in more than 200 countries and territories. The aggregate market value of PepsiCo, Inc. Common Stock held by nonaffiliates as of June 10, 2022, was $224.2 billion, based on the closing sale price on that date on the Nasdaq Global Select Market. The number of shares of PepsiCo, Inc. Common Stock outstanding as of February 2, 2023, was 1,377,251,316. Securities registered under Section 12(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 include Common Stock (symbol PEP), and Senior Notes due in 2024 (PEP24), 2026 (PEP26), 2027 (PEP27), 2028 (PEP28 and PEP28a), 2029 (PEP29), 2031 (PEP31), 2032 (PEP32), 2033 (PEP33), 2034 (PEP34), 2039 (PEP39), and 2050 (PEP50), all listed on the Nasdaq Stock Market LLC. The registrant is a well-known seasoned issuer, has filed all required reports during the preceding 12 months and for the past 90 days, has submitted electronically all required Interactive Data Files, is classified as a large accelerated filer, and has filed a report on and attestation to its management’s assessment of the effectiveness of internal control over financial reporting under Section 404(b) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act. The registrant is not a shell company. Portions of the Proxy Statement relating to PepsiCo, Inc.’s 2023 Annual Meeting of Shareholders are incorporated by reference into Part III of this Form 10-K.

PepsiCo retains a 39% noncontrolling interest in TBG, which operates across North America and Europe. In the first quarter of 2022, PepsiCo sold its Tropicana, Naked, and other select juice brands to PAI Partners while maintaining this 39% noncontrolling interest in TBG. In the United States, PepsiCo serves as the exclusive distributor for TBG’s portfolio of brands for small-format and foodservice customers with chilled direct-store-delivery (DSD). PepsiCo also began distributing Hard MTN Dew, an alcoholic beverage manufactured and owned by the Boston Beer Company, and has licensed the use of the Hard MTN Dew trademark to Boston Beer Company, which has appointed PepsiCo as its distributor for this product. AMESA, in either independent capacity or in conjunction with third parties, makes, markets, distributes, and sells convenient food brands such as Chipsy, Doritos, Kurkure, Lay’s, Sasko, Spekko, and White Star, as well as Quaker-branded convenient foods, and beverage concentrates, fountain syrups, and finished goods under brands including 7UP, Aquafina, Mirinda, Mountain Dew, and Pepsi. These products are sold to authorized and independent bottlers, independent distributors, and retailers, with AMESA operating its own bottling plants and distribution facilities in certain markets. AMESA also sells ready-to-drink tea products through an international joint venture with Unilever under the Lipton brand name. APAC, similarly, makes, markets, distributes, and sells convenient food brands including BaiCaoWei, Cheetos, Doritos, Lay’s, and Smith’s, along with Quaker-branded products, and beverage brands such as 7UP, Aquafina, Mirinda, Mountain Dew, Pepsi, and Sting, sold to authorized and independent bottlers, distributors, and retailers, and also sells ready-to-drink tea products through the same joint venture with Unilever under the Lipton brand. Products are distributed primarily through direct-store-delivery (DSD), customer warehouse systems, distributor networks, and e-commerce platforms and mobile applications, depending on customer needs, product characteristics, and local trade practices. Key ingredients include aspartame, corn, corn sweeteners, flavorings, flour, juice concentrates, oats, potatoes, raw milk, rice, seasonings, sucralose, sugar, vegetable and essential oils, and wheat, with water used in manufacturing. Packaging materials include polyethylene terephthalate (PET), polypropylene, aluminum, glass, closures, cardboard, and paperboard cartons. PepsiCo integrates recyclability into product development and supports recycled content, including recycled PET, in packaging. Fuel, electricity, and natural gas are essential commodities, and PepsiCo manages price fluctuations through fixed-price contracts, purchase orders, pricing agreements, and derivative instruments like swaps and futures. Supply risks are mitigated through purchases from multiple geographies and suppliers, and while price increases may or may not be passed on to customers, supply constraints due to the Ukraine conflict, the COVID-19 pandemic, inflation, adverse weather, supply chain disruptions, and labor shortages were experienced in 2022 and continued into fiscal 2023. PepsiCo maintains voluntary supply chain finance agreements with global financial institutions, allowing suppliers to sell their accounts receivable to these institutions, which had no material impact on business or financial results. PepsiCo owns numerous trademarks essential to its global operations, including Agusha, Amp Energy, Aquafina, Arto Lifewtr, Baja Blast, BaiCaoWei, Bare, Bokomo, bubly, Cap’n Crunch, Ceres, Cheetos, Chester’s, Chipsy, Chokis, Chudo, Cracker Jack, Crunchy, Diet Mountain Dew, Diet Mug, Diet Pepsi, Diet 7UP (outside the U.S.), Domik v Derevne, Doritos, Driftwell, Duyvis, Elma Chips, Emperador, Evolve, Frito-Lay, Fritos, Fruktovy Sad, G2, Gamesa, Gatorade, Gatorade Fit, Gatorade Zero, Gatorlyte, Grandma’s, H2oh!, Hard MTN Dew, Health Warrior, Imunele, J7, Kas, Kurkure, Lay’s, Life, Lifewtr, Liquifruit, Lubimy, Manzanita Sol, Marias Gamesa, Matutano, Mirinda, Miss Vickie’s, Moirs, Mother’s, Mountain Dew, Mountain Dew Code Red, Mountain Dew Game Fuel, Mountain Dew Kickstart, Mountain Dew Zero Sugar, MTN Dew Energy, Mug, Munchies, Muscle Milk, Near East, Off the Eaten Path, Paso de los Toros, Pasta Roni, Pearl Milling Company, Pepsi, Pepsi Black, Pepsi Max, Pepsi Zero Sugar, PopCorners, Pronutro, Propel, Quaker, Quaker Chewy, Quaker Simply Granola, Rice-A-Roni, Rockstar Energy, Rold Gold, Ruffles, Sabritas, Safari, Sakata, Saladitas Gamesa, San Carlos, Sandora, Santitas, Sasko, 7UP (outside the U.S.), 7UP Free (outside the U.S.), Sierra Mist, Sierra Mist Zero Sugar, Simba, Smartfood, Smith’s, Snack a Jacks, SoBe, SodaStream, Sonric’s, Spekko, Stacy’s, Starry, Sting, Stubborn Soda, SunChips, Toddy, Toddynho, Tostitos, V Water, Vesely Molochnik, Walkers, Weetbix, White Star, Ya, and Yachak. It also holds long-term licenses to use trademarks in certain markets, including Ocean Spray. PepsiCo distributes Celsius energy drinks and Keurig Dr Pepper Inc. brands such as Dr Pepper, Crush, and Schweppes. Joint ventures in which PepsiCo has an ownership interest either own or have rights to use trademarks such as Lipton, Sabra, and Starbucks. PepsiCo grants exclusive contracts to independent bottlers for the sale and manufacturing of certain beverage products in specific geographic areas, providing rights to charge royalties for concentrate, finished goods, and Aquafina, and specifying required manufacturing processes. Financial incentives are provided to customers, including volume-based rebates, product placement fees, promotions, and displays for independent distributors and retailers, and bottler funding for independent bottlers to support consumer incentives, advertising, new product launches, and vending equipment placement. Changes in the retail landscape, including retail consolidation, growth in e-commerce and subscription services, integration of digital and physical operations, and expansion of hard discounters, have increased the importance of major customers. In 2022, sales to Walmart Inc. and its affiliates, including Sam’s Club, represented approximately 14% of consolidated net revenue across all divisions, including concentrate sales to independent bottlers used in finished goods sold to Walmart; the loss of this customer would have a material adverse effect on the FLNA, QFNA, and PBNA divisions. PepsiCo competes in highly competitive beverage and convenient food markets against international companies, regional and local manufacturers, private label brands, and micro brands sold via e-commerce or local retailers. The Coca-Cola Company is PepsiCo’s primary beverage competitor in many markets, including the U.S., where in 2022, PepsiCo and Coca-Cola represented approximately 20% and 21% of the U.S. liquid refreshment beverage category by retail sales, respectively. Coca-Cola holds a significant carbonated soft drink share advantage outside the U.S. Competition is based on brand recognition, loyalty, taste, price, value, quality, product variety, innovation, distribution, advertising, marketing, packaging, convenience, service, and responsiveness to consumer trends such as health and wellness and sustainability, as well as e-commerce growth. Success depends on effective promotion, new product development and reformulations, production efficiency, technology integration, advertising, packaging, pricing, vending equipment, and brand protection. PepsiCo conducts global research and development focused on creating consumer-preferred products through new technologies, ingredients, flavors, and substrates; improving manufacturing processes to reduce cost and environmental impact; reducing added sugars, sodium, and saturated fat; offering functional ingredients like whole grains, fruits, vegetables, dairy, protein, fiber, and micronutrients; developing sustainable packaging, including recyclable, compostable, or biodegradable options; advancing marketing and dispensing equipment; expanding beyond-the-bottle offerings, such as for SodaStream; investing in artificial intelligence and data analytics; strengthening omnichannel capabilities, especially in e-commerce; and reducing environmental impact through water conservation and sustainable agricultural practices. Research centers are located in Brazil, China, India, Ireland, Mexico, Russia, South Africa, the United Kingdom, and the United States. PepsiCo’s operations are subject to various federal, state, and local laws in the U.S. and over 200 other countries, including the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, Food Safety Modernization Act, Occupational Safety and Health Act, environmental protection laws, Federal Motor Carrier Safety Act, Federal Trade Commission Act, Lanham Act, competition and trade laws, employment laws, alcohol sale and distribution laws, data privacy regulations such as the California Consumer Privacy Act, customs and trade laws, and the 2010 California Transparency in Supply Chains Act. PepsiCo adheres to all applicable global laws and regulations.

PepsiCo is subject to a wide range of federal, state, and local laws and regulations that govern workplace health and safety, employment practices, environmental protection, competition, trade practices, product labeling, data privacy, and supply chain operations. These include the Equal Employment Opportunity Act, the National Labor Relations Act, the Fair Labor Standards Act, the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Act, the Federal Trade Commission Act, the Lanham Act, the Robinson-Patman Act, and the Clayton Act. The company also complies with laws related to the sale and distribution of alcohol, data privacy regulations such as the California Consumer Privacy Act of 2018 (as modified by the California Privacy Rights Act), and international trade laws, including customs regulations, tariffs, and laws governing the import or export of products and ingredients. PepsiCo is required to comply with the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act and the Trade Sanctions Reform and Export Enhancement Act. In addition, it is subject to state and local statutes such as Proposition 65 in California, which mandates warnings on products containing substances known to cause cancer or birth defects if above a safe harbor level. The company also faces regulations outside the United States, including food safety laws, international trade, supply chain rules like the U.K. Modern Slavery Act, occupational health and safety, competition, anti-corruption (including the U.K. Bribery Act), and data privacy (such as the European Union General Data Protection Regulation). Compliance with competition and anti-corruption laws is especially important due to PepsiCo’s competitive position in many jurisdictions. The company relies on legal and operational compliance programs, in-house and external legal counsel, and other experts to ensure adherence to global laws. Certain jurisdictions have imposed or are considering imposing new or increased taxes on the manufacture, distribution, or sale of PepsiCo’s products, ingredients, or substances, with tax structures varying—some applying to all beverages, others to those with caloric sweeteners, and some using flat, graduated, or per-ounce/liter rates based on added sugar or specific ingredients. Additionally, product labeling, marketing, and sales restrictions are being introduced or considered, including warnings about ingredients, age restrictions, and geographic limitations on product availability. Regulations to increase recycling, reduce waste, or restrict packaging—such as deposit return systems, extended producer responsibility policies, or bans on single-use plastics and PFAS-containing packaging—are also in place or under consideration. PepsiCo is subject to U.S. and foreign environmental laws, including the Clean Air Act, Clean Water Act, Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation and Liability Act, and the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act, as well as similar laws abroad. Ongoing concerns about climate change, water scarcity, and environmental, social, and governance (ESG) metrics are expected to lead to new or stricter regulatory requirements, which the company addresses through internal environmental compliance programs and planned expenditures. While these costs have not materially impacted financial performance to date, future changes could adversely affect results. The company also faces environmental remediation and indemnification obligations from historical activities or acquisitions, which are not expected to have a material impact on capital expenditures, earnings, or competitive position. PepsiCo employs approximately 315,000 people worldwide as of December 31, 2022, including about 132,000 in the United States, and maintains good relations with employees through numerous collective bargaining agreements. Protecting employee safety and health is a top priority, with investments in technologies such as fleet telematics, distracted driving prevention, ergonomic solutions, and machine safety to reduce workplace injuries. During the COVID-19 pandemic, the company implemented safety protocols, provided personal protective equipment, and enabled testing, and has also supported employees and communities in Ukraine through humanitarian aid. PepsiCo believes its culture of diversity, equity, and inclusion is a competitive advantage, with approximately 27% of its global workforce being female and 44% of management roles held by women as of December 31, 2022. About 48% of its U.S. workforce is racially/ethnically diverse, and 33% of U.S. managerial associates are racially/ethnically diverse. The Board has overseen appointments of seven globally diverse or female executives directly reporting to the Chief Executive Officer. The company supports associate development through global training programs, career development plans, mentoring, and in-house learning such as PEP U Degreed, with over 1 million training hours completed in 2022. PepsiCo files annual, quarterly, and current reports, proxy statements, and other disclosures with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), and these filings are available on the SEC’s website and on its corporate website at http://www.pepsico.com. The company communicates material information through SEC filings, press releases, public conference calls, webcasts, and its corporate website, and encourages stakeholders to review this information. The information on the website is not incorporated into any SEC filings. The document also includes a section on risk factors, highlighting risks such as the ongoing conflict in Ukraine, which has caused supply chain disruptions, increased costs, reputational risks, and business interruptions, and could impact demand for products. Demand for PepsiCo’s products depends on its ability to anticipate and respond to evolving consumer trends, including preferences for product quality, packaging, nutrition, and health concerns, as well as shifts in demographics, e-commerce, and channel preferences. Pandemics, such as COVID-19, have influenced consumer behavior and demand. Any failure to adapt to changing consumer preferences or to respond effectively to trends can reduce demand, lead to inventory write-offs, and harm competitive positioning. Damage to the company’s reputation—due to ethical lapses, environmental or social issues, product safety concerns, advertising, or social media responses—can reduce consumer demand. Product recalls due to quality, safety, or labeling issues, including those involving allergens, contamination, or misbranding, can result in financial losses, inventory destruction, lost sales, and reputational damage, especially as the company expands into new categories like alcoholic beverages. Failure to maintain oversight can lead to litigation, investigations, fines, or criminal liability. PepsiCo competes with international beverage and food companies, regional brands, private labels, and e-commerce-based microbrands, primarily on brand loyalty, taste, price, innovation, distribution, and marketing. The company’s ability to compete effectively depends on its capacity to promote existing products, launch new ones, adopt new technologies like artificial intelligence and data analytics, and respond to consumer trends.

Our business can be adversely affected by a range of factors, including fines, penalties, damages, or criminal liability, particularly if consumers lose confidence in product quality, safety, or integrity—regardless of whether such concerns relate directly to our products. We face competition from international beverage and convenient food companies, regional and local manufacturers, private label and economy brands, and smaller firms selling micro brands directly to consumers via e-commerce or locally focused retailers. In many countries, including the United States, The Coca-Cola Company is our primary competitor. We compete based on brand recognition, loyalty, taste, price, value, quality, product variety, innovation, distribution, advertising, marketing, packaging, convenience, service, and our ability to anticipate and respond to consumer preferences. Failure to effectively promote or develop existing products, introduce or market new ones, adopt new technologies like artificial intelligence and data analytics, strengthen digital marketing capabilities, or respond to supply disruptions, pricing pressure (including from commodity inflation), or competitive actions—such as aggressive spending by rivals—can harm our business. We may also struggle to grow or maintain sales or category share, requiring increased capital, marketing, or other expenditures. Our success depends on attracting, developing, and retaining a highly skilled and diverse workforce, as employees are highly sought after by competitors, and labor market challenges such as wage inflation, labor shortages, employee turnover, shifts to remote work, and ineffective succession planning—especially for leadership roles like the Chief Executive Officer—can erode our competitive edge, increase costs, and damage our reputation. Water scarcity poses a significant risk, as we and our partners use water in manufacturing and raw material production; shortages, regulatory pressures, climate change, or conservation efforts can disrupt supply chains, increase compliance and production costs, lead to facility shutdowns or relocations, impair our water use goals, and harm our reputation. Changes in the retail landscape—such as growth in e-commerce and hard discounters—can negatively impact us if we fail to maintain relationships with these channels or traditional retailers, especially as key customers like Walmart increase their e-commerce presence. Consolidation among large retailers or buying groups reduces our competitive ability and weakens smaller customers’ purchasing power, potentially leading to lost orders or reduced sales. Disruptions in manufacturing or supply chains, including rising costs for commodities, packaging, transportation, labor, and other inputs—due to civil unrest, political instability, supplier constraints, seasonal shortages, natural disasters, pandemics, strikes, tariffs, port congestion, or cybersecurity incidents—can increase costs and interrupt product supply. Political and social conditions, including election outcomes, government shutdowns, hostilities, protests, and climate-related events, can create uncertainty in regulations, affect demand, and disrupt operations. Our ability to grow in developing and emerging markets—such as Mexico, the Middle East, China, South Africa, Brazil, and India—is uncertain due to competition, cultural differences, distribution challenges, economic instability, inflation, currency fluctuations, foreign ownership restrictions, nationalization risks, trade barriers, and complex compliance requirements, including under the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, the U.K. Bribery Act, and the Trade Sanctions Reform and Export Enhancement Act. Adverse economic conditions, such as inflation, interest rate changes, tax shifts, recessions, volatile commodity markets, credit contraction, or currency devaluation, can negatively impact our operations and those of our business partners. Cyber incidents, including cyberattacks, network outages, software failures, employee errors, or natural disasters—especially as remote work increases our IT vulnerability—can disrupt operations, compromise data, lead to financial losses, litigation, regulatory penalties, reputational damage, or employee morale issues. These risks extend to third-party providers, including suppliers and cloud service providers, who may introduce malware through software updates or compromised accounts, and whose systems may be exploited or fail, indirectly affecting our business. Although past cyber incidents have not materially impacted our operations, future events could do so. Despite significant investments in network security, disaster recovery, and employee training, there is no guarantee these measures will prevent all incidents, and insurance may not cover all losses or reputational harm. Finally, failure to successfully complete or manage strategic transactions—such as acquisitions, joint ventures, divestitures, or refranchisings—due to integration challenges, unmet synergies, regulatory hurdles, tax inefficiencies, or differing interests among partners can also harm our business.

Our ability to achieve the full expected returns, benefits, cost savings, or synergies from strategic transactions within the anticipated time frame or at all, including obtaining necessary consents, clearances, and approvals, is subject to significant risks. These risks include difficulties in integrating manufacturing, distribution, sales, accounting, financial reporting, and administrative support activities and information technology systems with our company, or challenges in separating such functions during divestitures; operating under new business models or in new categories or territories; motivating, recruiting, and retaining executives and key employees; conforming to controls and policies related to financial reporting, disclosure, data protection, cybersecurity, environmental compliance, health and safety, and anti-bribery laws; retaining existing customers and attracting new ones; managing tax costs or inefficiencies; maintaining good relations with divested or refranchised businesses in our supply or sales chain; offsetting revenue losses from divested brands or businesses; managing the impact of decisions or actions by joint venture partners with differing interests; and facing unanticipated problems or liabilities such as contingent liabilities or litigation. Poorly executed or poorly managed strategic transactions have in the past and could continue to harm our business. We rely on third-party service providers, including cloud data providers, for payroll processing, health and benefit administration, and certain finance and accounting functions. Failure by these providers to meet their contractual, regulatory, or other obligations, or our failure to adequately monitor their performance, can lead to inability to achieve expected cost savings or efficiencies, additional correction costs, business disruptions, systems performance degradation, processing inefficiencies, security breaches, incorrect or adverse financial reporting, litigation, claims, regulatory proceedings, fines, penalties, reputational damage, or negative employee morale—all of which can adversely affect our business. We are also implementing a multi-year phased business transformation to migrate financial processing systems to enterprise-wide solutions, which has led to and could continue to result in systems outages and operating inefficiencies. If we fail to allocate and manage the necessary resources to build and sustain the required IT infrastructure or fail to achieve expected benefits from this initiative, our business could be harmed. Climate change poses risks by increasing the frequency or severity of natural disasters, extreme weather, and disruptions to agricultural production, affecting the availability and pricing of key commodities like potatoes, sugar cane, corn, wheat, rice, oats, and oranges. Increased regulatory focus on climate change, greenhouse gas emissions, energy policies, and sustainability—including single-use plastics—may introduce new or stricter legal and regulatory requirements, such as carbon pricing or revised labeling, leading to significant increased costs and investment needs. Failure to meet or properly report on environmental goals or to respond effectively to climate-related regulations can result in adverse publicity, reduced demand, reputational damage, or litigation. Strikes or work stoppages, due to inability to renew or enter into satisfactory collective bargaining agreements with employees or third parties involved in manufacturing, production, or distribution, can impair product supply, lead to lost sales, increased costs, and disrupt operational changes, all of which can harm our business. Our financial performance depends on our ability to implement productivity initiatives, such as shared business service models, to reduce costs and improve efficiency. However, these initiatives may cause business disruptions, management distraction, reduced morale, unexpected attrition, difficulty attracting or retaining key personnel, and negative publicity. If we fail to achieve expected savings, we may not realize anticipated benefits, negatively impacting financial performance. We conduct annual or more frequent impairment tests on goodwill and indefinite-lived intangible assets, and evaluate amortizable intangible assets, property, plant, and equipment for impairment when there is a significant change in operating or macroeconomic conditions. Deterioration in assumptions about competitive conditions, macroeconomic factors, or the weighted-average cost of capital can result in impairment charges, adversely affecting results of operations. Exchange rate fluctuations, due to inflation, monetary policies, currency controls, or restrictions, impact our financial performance because our consolidated financial statements are in U.S. dollars and we operate globally, paying for raw materials and ingredients in multiple currencies. A downgrade or potential downgrade of our credit ratings—based on factors such as cash generation, indebtedness, shareholder distributions, and broader economic or industry conditions—can increase borrowing costs, impair access to capital and credit markets, reduce liquidity, and limit our ability to access commercial paper at favorable rates, all of which can harm financial performance. Certain jurisdictions have imposed or are considering new or increased taxes on our products, especially beverages, due to ingredients like sugar, with examples including Italy’s flat tax of EUR 10 cents per liter on all beverages effective January 1, 2023. These taxes can increase product costs, reduce consumption, and lead to negative publicity. Similarly, limitations on marketing or sale of our products—such as warning labels, age restrictions, or location bans—have been introduced in places like Brazil and Canada, and color-coded labeling is being considered, which may reduce consumption, cause negative publicity, or lead consumers to perceive our products as not meeting health needs. Laws and regulations regarding plastic or packaging materials—such as extended producer responsibility, plastic taxes, bans on single-use plastics or PFAS-containing packaging, bottle cap tethering, or recycling requirements—have been implemented or are under consideration in the EU, Peru, and U.S. states, increasing product costs, impacting demand, and requiring capital investments to reduce virgin plastic use, develop alternative packaging, or revise labeling. Failure to comply with personal data protection and privacy laws—such as the California Consumer Privacy Act, California Privacy Rights Act, Virginia, Colorado, Utah, Connecticut, EU’s GDPR, and China’s PIPL—creates significant compliance costs and challenges, with non-compliance leading to litigation, fines, reputational damage, and regulatory scrutiny. Increases in income tax rates, changes in tax laws, or disagreements with tax authorities can adversely affect financial performance, especially given global trends like the OECD’s proposed global minimum tax of 15% and EU adoption of such rules, which may not be adopted universally and could still negatively impact us. The increasingly complex global tax environment increases tax uncertainty, compliance costs, and the difficulty of resolving tax audits or disputes, which may result in outcomes different from historical provisions. We also face risks related to intellectual property, including failure to protect our ingredient formulas, trademarks, patents, trade secrets, or business processes, or allegations of infringing on others’ rights, which could lead to costly litigation, reputational harm, operational disruptions, injunctions, inventory write-offs, or restrictions on product development and sales. Our business is subject to numerous laws and regulations covering production, storage, distribution, sale, advertising, labeling, content (including genetically engineered ingredients), quality, safety, transportation, traceability, sourcing, packaging, disposal, recycling, employment, environmental, social, and governance matters, and data privacy. Compliance with competition and anti-corruption laws is especially critical due to our competitive position. New laws, changes in regulations, evolving enforcement priorities, or differing standards across markets can increase compliance and capital costs, necessitate product reformulation, or otherwise harm our business. Growing societal and governmental attention to environmental, social, and governance issues has led to expanded disclosure requirements, increasing the scope and complexity of reporting obligations. Additionally, entering new markets or categories, such as the alcoholic beverage industry as a distributor, has introduced and may continue to introduce new regulatory and compliance challenges.

Social and governance matters, including climate change and data privacy and protection, are significant areas of focus for the company. In many jurisdictions, compliance with competition and antitrust laws and anti-corruption laws is particularly important due to the company’s competitive position. Changes in laws, regulatory requirements, or enforcement priorities, as well as differing or competing regulations across markets where products are made, manufactured, distributed, or sold, can lead to higher compliance costs, capital expenditures, and production costs, or necessitate product reformulation, which may negatively impact the business. Increased governmental and societal attention to environmental, social, and governance issues has led to and may continue to result in new laws and expanded disclosure requirements, increasing the scope and complexity of reporting obligations. The entry into new markets or categories, such as the alcoholic beverage industry as a distributor, has resulted in and may continue to result in additional regulatory exposure and higher compliance costs. If one jurisdiction imposes new laws or regulations affecting the manufacture, distribution, or sale of products, other jurisdictions may follow. Failure to comply with such laws or regulations—or allegations thereof—can lead to criminal or civil investigations, enforcement actions, including document requests, fines, injunctions, product recalls, penalties, disgorgement of profits, or activity restrictions, all of which can harm the business. Third-party studies, whether scientifically valid or not, claiming health implications from certain ingredients or packaging materials have resulted in and may continue to result in new taxes, regulations, or lawsuits that adversely affect the business. Potential liabilities from litigation, claims, legal or regulatory proceedings, inquiries, or investigations can negatively impact the business. The company and its subsidiaries are involved in various legal matters, including those related to advertising, marketing, product labels, ingredients, personal injury, property damage, intellectual property, privacy, employment, tax, insurance, environmental, social, and governance issues, and compliance with applicable laws. These matters are inherently uncertain, and there is no guarantee of successful defense or that the company’s assessment of materiality, potential losses, or reserves will match the ultimate outcomes. Responding to these matters, even if ultimately non-meritorious, requires significant expense and resource allocation and may damage the company’s reputation or brand image. Regarding unresolved staff comments, the company has received no written comments from the SEC staff regarding periodic or current reports issued 180 days or more before the end of the 2022 fiscal year that remain unresolved. The company’s principal executive office is in Purchase, New York, and its facilities in Plano, Texas, which it owns, are its most significant corporate properties. Each division uses manufacturing, processing, bottling, production plants, warehouses, distribution centers, storage facilities, offices, research and development facilities, and other facilities, either owned or leased. Significant properties by division include: a research and development facility in Plano, Texas (owned); a convenient food plant in Cedar Rapids, Iowa (owned); a research and development facility in Valhalla, New York (owned); a concentrate plant in Arlington, Texas (owned); a convenient food plant in Celaya, Mexico (owned); two convenient food plants in Vallejo, Mexico (owned); a convenient food plant in Leicester, United Kingdom (leased); a manufacturing plant in Lehavim, Israel (owned); a dairy plant in Moscow, Russia (owned); a convenient food plant in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia (owned); a convenient food plant in Wuhan, China (owned); a shared service center in Winston Salem, North Carolina (leased); a concentrate plant in Colonia, Uruguay (owned); two concentrate plants in Cork, Ireland (owned); a concentrate plant in Singapore (owned); and a shared service center in Hyderabad, India (leased). A Member is entitled to an Early Retirement Pension if employment with both the Employer and the PepsiCo Organization terminates on or after age 55 but before Normal Retirement Age and after completing 10 or more years of Service; the Annuity Starting Date is ordinarily the Normal Retirement Date, but the Member may file a written election with the Vice President to set it as the first day of any month after termination but before Normal Retirement Date; the Pension amount is computed as if retiring at Normal Retirement Age using the Member’s Highest Average Monthly Salary (as defined in Table A) and Pensionable Service as of termination date, but if the Pension is received before age 62, it is reduced by 4/12 of 1 percent for each month before the Member would have reached age 62. A Member may be entitled to a Special Early Retirement Pension if employment terminates on or after age 50 but before age 55, after completing at least 10 years of Service, and only if authorized by the Vice President; the Annuity Starting Date is the first day of the month after the Vice President authorizes the Special Early Retirement Pension; the Pension amount is computed as if retiring at Normal Retirement Age using the Member’s Highest Average Monthly Salary and Pensionable Service as of termination date, but is reduced by 4/12 of 1 percent for each month before the Member would have reached age 62. Section 4.04 Deferred Vested Pension begins with (a).

A Member may be entitled to a Special Early Retirement Pension if their employment with both their Employer and the PepsiCo Organization ends on or after age 50 but before age 55 and after completing at least 10 years of Service, provided such pension is authorized by the Vice President. The Annuity Starting Date for this pension is the first day of the month following the Vice President’s authorization. The pension amount is calculated using Table A as if the Member retired at their Normal Retirement Date, based on their Highest Average Monthly Salary and Pensionable Service as of their employment termination date, but is reduced by 4/12 of 1 percent for each month the pension commences before the Member would have reached age 62. A Member who terminates employment with both their Employer and the PepsiCo Organization before becoming eligible for a Normal Retirement Pension, Early Retirement Pension, or Special Early Retirement Pension may be entitled to a Deferred Vested Pension if they meet the vesting requirements in Sections 4.06 or 4.07. The amount of the Deferred Vested Pension is determined in accordance with Table A using the Member’s Highest Average Monthly Salary at termination (subject to Sections 9.13 and 9.14) and their Pensionable Service as of termination. The pension commences on the later of (i) the termination of employment or (ii) the Member’s Normal Retirement Date, though the Member may elect, by filing a written election with the Vice President, to have it commence on the first day of any month after the Member attains age 55 (or after termination, if later). If the Member receives the pension before their Normal Retirement Date, the amount is reduced according to the reduction factors for early commencement of a “Vested Pension” under the PepsiCo Salaried Plan, not those for Early or Special Early Retirement Pensions. If the Member becomes entitled to a Deferred Vested Pension and later becomes an Eligible Employee again, they are re-admitted to Active Membership under Article III, and their prior Service and Pensionable Service are aggregated with subsequent Service and Pensionable Service for pension calculations upon later retirement, provided the prior pension was not previously cashed out under Section 5.05. A Member who continues employment with the PepsiCo Organization or any Employer after reaching their Normal Retirement Age is entitled to a Late Retirement Pension, with the Annuity Starting Date being the first day of the month coincident with or immediately following termination of employment with both the Employer and PepsiCo Organization. The Member is credited with Salary and Pensionable Service after their Normal Retirement Date unless otherwise prospectively determined by the Vice President. A Member is fully vested in their Pension upon completing 5 years of Service or, if earlier, upon death or disability while employed, with disability determined by the Vice President using standards deemed appropriate at the time. An Active Member who will have an Approved Transfer during a Plan Year automatically achieves special vesting as of the last business day before the earlier of (a) the Approved Transfer or (b) the day they would become a U.S. Person in connection with the transfer. Similarly, an Active Member may request special vesting as of the last business day before a Status Change, with both the request and Vice President’s approval required to be final and in place prior to the date of application. The effect of special vesting under either (a) or (b) is that the Member becomes vested to the same extent as under Section 4.06, subject to the requirement that benefits remain exempt from Section 409A of the Internal Revenue Code and that this Section 4.07 does not apply to the extent inconsistent with that requirement. A Member who earns Service and Pensionable Service after their Annuity Starting Date under prior Sections of Article IV (excluding a cashout under Section 5.05) will have any prior suspended benefits and additional accrued benefits paid at their subsequent Annuity Starting Date. The suspension or continuation of prior benefits, adjustments to benefits at the subsequent Annuity Starting Date, and elections of payment time and form are subject to rules established by the Vice President, based on the PepsiCo Salaried Plan’s rules for benefits accrued after benefit commencement, unless the Vice President determines a modification is appropriate. Under Article V, distribution options include normal forms of payment: unmarried Members receive a Single Life Annuity unless they elect otherwise; married Members receive a 50 Percent Survivor Annuity unless they elect otherwise, with the pension amount reduced by 10 percent for Annuity Starting Dates before January 1, 2019, except for members entitled to a pension under the Plan prior to January 1, 1990, whose pension is not subject to this reduction. For Annuity Starting Dates on or after January 1, 2019, the pension amount is reduced to its Actuarial Equivalent to reflect the survivor benefit. Married Members may also elect optional forms of payment, including a Single Life Annuity or a 75 Percent Survivor Annuity, regardless of eligibility for other options. Survivor options include a 100 Percent Survivor Option (with a 20 percent reduction for pre-January 1, 2019, starting dates, subject to subsection (f)), a 75 Percent Survivor Option (with a 15 percent reduction for pre-January 1, 2019, starting dates), and a 50 Percent Survivor Option (with a 10 percent reduction for pre-January 1, 2019, starting dates, not applicable to members entitled to a pension prior to January 1, 1990). A Ten-Year Certain and Life Option allows monthly payments for at least 120 months, with post-death payments to a primary or contingent Dependant or estate, and effective January 1, 2010, the Dependant or estate may elect a lump sum equal to the actuarial equivalent of remaining payments (without mortality reduction). A Lump Sum Payment option allows a single lump sum equal to the actuarial equivalent of the Single Life Annuity, calculated using lump sum equivalent factors from the PepsiCo Salaried Plan (excluding transition factors), paid within one taxable year and as soon as practicable after the Member’s specified date, with interest added to late payments after January 1, 2010, but no interest during any deferred period. A Combination Lump Sum/Monthly Benefit allows a portion in lump sum and the remainder in monthly payments, with the percentages adding to 100 percent. The lump sum amount is calculated by multiplying the amount under Section 5.03(c) by the designated lump sum percentage, and the monthly amount by the designated monthly percentage. If a Member entitled to an immediate pension under Article IV elects an optional form of payment and dies after leaving employment but before the pension becomes payable, the optional form of payment begins on the first day of the month following death.

The amount of a lump sum benefit is determined by multiplying the amount established under Section 5.03(c) by the percentage the Member has designated for receipt as a lump sum. The amount of a monthly benefit is calculated by multiplying the monthly benefit elected by the Member, as determined under Sections 5.03(a) or (b), by the percentage designated for monthly payments. If a Member entitled to an immediate Pension under Article IV elects an optional form of payment under Section 5.03 and meets all requirements (excluding survival, but including timely election and any required consent from an Eligible Spouse), and dies after leaving employment but before the Pension becomes payable, the optional form of payment is deemed effective on the first day of the month following death. This deemed effectiveness applies only once and only to the initial election, except as permitted by a prior decision of the Vice President regarding a subsequent purported election. However, for the option under Section 5.03(b), if the specified Dependant dies or shall die before the first installment of the Pension is prospectively payable under the elected form, the election is not effective. For annuities starting before January 1, 2019, if a Dependant is more than 10 years younger than the Member, the Pension is reduced: if the Dependant is more than 10 but not more than 20 years younger, the reduction percentage is increased by 5 percentage points; if the Dependant is more than 20 years younger, the 5 percentage point increase is further increased by an additional 0.2 percent for each full year over 20. Section 5.04 restricts certain distribution options: the form in Section 5.03(d) is not available unless the Member’s Annuity Starting Date is after 1989; Deferred Vested Pensions under Section 4.04 are eligible only for the Single Life Annuity, the 50 Percent Survivor Option, or the 75 Percent Survivor Option, except that effective January 1, 2015, they may also be eligible for the Lump Sum Payment option, but only if available on an ongoing basis under the PepsiCo Salaried Plan, and participants in the PepsiCo Pension Equalization Plan are not excluded from this option. For Members who became entitled to a Pension before January 1, 1990, actuarial equivalencies are adjusted by the Vice President to reflect the value of any subsidized survivor benefit under Section 5.02(b). Under Section 5.05, if the total Pension payable is deemed relatively trivial by the Vice President, the entire Pension may be commuted to a lump sum payable after the Member’s termination of employment from both employer and PepsiCo Organization, or after a transfer within PepsiCo that ends accrual of DB benefits, on a date set by the Vice President without Member consent. Effective January 1, 2019, the Vice President may make a lump-sum payment to any Member whose benefit has commenced (not in lump sum form) if the present value of the remaining payments is less than or equal to $75,000 on the payment date; the lump sum amount equals the actuarial equivalent of the remaining payments, calculated using the lump sum equivalent factors in Section 5.03(c) as of a date set by the Vice President. A Member who elects a payment form with a survivor option must designate a Dependant entitled to benefits upon death; the designation may be changed or revoked at any time before the election’s effective date. If the Member is married at the time of designation, naming a Dependant other than the Eligible Spouse requires the Eligible Spouse’s written consent; revocation of a Dependant does not require consent. All designations, changes, revocations, and consents must be in writing on forms provided by the Vice President and filed with the Vice President to be effective. For the survivor option in Section 5.03(b)(4), the Member may name both a primary and a contingent Dependant; if no Dependant is properly designated, the election is not effective. Under Article VI, a surviving Eligible Spouse or Eligible Domestic Partner is entitled to survivor benefits if the requirements are met, with the benefit amount determined according to Section II of Table A. For an Active Member, a Member in Service after Normal Retirement Date with at least 5 years of Service, or a Member entitled to an Early Retirement Pension or Special Early Retirement Pension who is survived by an Eligible Spouse or Domestic Partner and not entitled to protection under Section 5.03(e), a Pre-Retirement Spouse’s or Domestic Partner’s Pension is payable, calculated under Section II of Table A. For a vested Member not covered in Section 6.01, who has not yet commenced or received a Pension, and who is survived by an Eligible Spouse or Domestic Partner and not entitled to protection under Section 5.03(e), a Pre-Retirement Spouse’s or Domestic Partner’s Pension is payable, calculated based on the Member’s Salary and Pensionable Service as of the earlier of death or termination of employment, as if the Member had lived until the earliest date their vested benefit could have started with a 50 Percent Survivor Annuity and died that day. This benefit is paid by reducing the monthly benefit otherwise payable to the Member, using the same methodology and factors as in the PepsiCo Salaried Plan, and the Member may only waive this coverage with Vice President approval. Any Pension payable under Article VI is payable for the surviving Eligible Spouse or Domestic Partner’s life only, except that if the Member was eligible for a Normal, Early, or Special Early Retirement Pension at death, the surviving spouse or partner may elect a single lump sum payment instead of an annuity. The benefit commences on the first day of the month coinciding with or next following the Member’s death, or if later, the date the Member would have reached age 55; if the benefit commences before the Member would have reached Normal Retirement Age, it is reduced as set forth in Sections 4.02, 4.03, or 4.04, as applicable. Any benefit subject to disposition under Article VI is held by the Vice President, who has the power to pay or apply it to or for the benefit of one or more of the Member’s dependants as they see fit, and may direct the benefit to commence or be paid as a lump sum as soon as practicable after the Member’s death. The Plan is administered by the Vice President, who has the authority to interpret the Plan and issue regulations, and all actions and interpretations are final and binding. The Vice President may delegate responsibilities to others, and any reference to the Vice President may refer to a delegate or designated person. If a person entitled to a benefit is legally disabled or incapacitated, the Vice President may direct payments to a legal representative or apply them for the person’s benefit, and such payment constitutes a complete discharge of liability. The Vice President has exclusive discretionary authority to interpret the Plan, determine eligibility and benefit amounts, and all decisions are final and conclusive. This discretion is absolute and will be reviewed under the arbitrary and capricious standard by a court, arbitrator, or tribunal. If a claim for benefits is denied, the Vice President or a designated party must provide a written notice within 90 days that includes the specific reasons for denial, references to relevant Plan provisions, a description of any additional material needed to perfect the claim, and a description of the claim review procedure, including time limits. If special circumstances require an extension, the period may be extended from 90 to 180 days, with notice given before the end of the initial 90-day period. Upon review, the Vice President must provide a full and fair review, including the opportunity to submit comments, documents, and records, and the review must consider such submissions regardless of whether they were considered initially. The decision on review is made within 60 days after receipt of the request, unless extended by up to an additional 60 days with prior notice. The final decision must be in writing, understandable to the claimant, include specific reasons and references to Plan provisions, and provide that the claimant is entitled, upon request and free of charge, to copies of all relevant documents, records, and information. Any claim reviewed by a court, arbitrator, or tribunal is reviewed solely on the record before the Vice President’s initial determination and only after the claimant has fully exhausted all rights under this section and Section 7.07. Any claim filed under Article VII or any action in court or tribunal by a former or current Employee, Member, Dependant, or other individual must be brought within two years of when the cause of action first accrues, which is deemed to be not later than the earlier of (i) when the claimant receives the benefit calculation, (ii) the date identified by the Vice President for payment commencement, or (iii) when the claimant has actual or constructive knowledge of the facts underlying the claim. Failure to file within this two-year period precludes the claim or action.

Any claim for the alleged wrongful denial of Plan benefits by a former or current Employee, Member, Dependant, or any other individual, person, or entity (a “Petitioner”) must be filed within two years of the date the Petitioner’s cause of action first accrues. For this purpose, a cause of action accrues not later than the earlier of (i) when the Petitioner receives the calculation of the benefits at issue, (ii) the date identified by the Vice President on which payments are to commence, or (iii) when the Petitioner has actual or constructive knowledge of the facts supporting the claim. Failure to file within this two-year period will preclude the Petitioner or any representative from bringing the claim. Communications following the mandatory appeals process described in Section 7.03 do not extend or affect this two-year limitation. Any claim or action related to the Plan must be brought only in the state or federal courts of New York, specifically the one nearest the Corporation’s headquarters. Specific references in the Plan to the Vice President’s discretion do not imply that such discretion is less broad in any other context. Before filing any claim, suit, or action in court or another tribunal, a Claimant must first fully exhaust all rights under the claims procedure in Section 7.03. This exhaustion requirement applies regardless of whether other Disputes are more significant, to any rights the Vice President may provide, whether actual or potential, and even if no specific procedures exist for the claim—where no procedures exist, the Vice President must either promptly establish them or apply the procedures in Section 7.03. The Vice President may make special arrangements to consider claims on a class basis or address unusual conflicts, but such arrangements must ensure exhaustion is required to the maximum extent. A “Dispute” includes any claim, issue, assertion, or matter, and a “Claim” is any Dispute that involves (A) the interpretation of the Plan, (B) any term or condition of the Plan, (C) the interpretation of the Plan in light of applicable law, (D) whether the Plan has been validly adopted, (E) the administration of the Plan, (F) whether the Plan has violated applicable law or regulation, (G) a request for or attempt to recover Plan benefits, (H) an assertion of a legal duty, or (I) any claim deemed similar by the Vice President or relating to the Plan. A “Claimant” includes any actual or putative Eligible Employee, former Employee, Member, former Member, Dependant, spouse, former spouse, estate, heir, or representative thereof, or any other individual, person, or entity with a relationship to such individuals or the Plan, or a group of such individuals. The Vice President intends to interpret and operate the Plan in good faith and in compliance with applicable law, and the requirement to exhaust claims is contractual and intended to ensure efficient, uniform resolution and to prevent substantial litigation costs. While the Corporation intends to continue the Plan indefinitely, it makes no contractual commitment to do so and reserves the right to amend, terminate, or partially terminate the Plan at any time, provided that no such action adversely affects the benefit amount of a Member or Dependant on the date of amendment or termination, unless the Member becomes entitled to an equivalent benefit under another Corporation plan or practice. Specific forms of payment are not protected. Amendments may be made by the Corporation in its sole discretion, with or without retroactive effect, and no Employer other than the Corporation may amend the Plan. If the Plan is terminated with respect to fewer than all Employers, it continues for the benefit of employees of the remaining Employers. The Employers’ obligations under the Plan are unfunded and constitute liabilities payable from their general funds, and rights to benefits are no greater than those of unsecured general creditors. All costs, charges, and expenses of Plan administration are borne by the Employers and allocated based on the proportion of Members employed by each Employer. If a Member is absent from duty for reasons other than death, discharge, retirement, or quitting (e.g., sickness, accident, layoff, vacation), they are deemed to have terminated employment 12 months after the absence begins, unless the Vice President determines otherwise. If the absence is due to full-time service in the armed forces or national service, the Member is not deemed terminated so long as the Employer considers them in employment or until they resign permanently, whichever occurs first. If the Vice President determines that a benefit is subject to a tax or assessment, the Plan may withhold up to the amount of such tax or duty from the benefit and apply it to satisfy the obligation. Nothing in the Plan constitutes a contract of employment, a right to continue employment, or a limitation on an Employer’s right to discharge employees. No person has a claim, right, or interest under the Plan except as provided in the Plan, and termination of employment is not grounds for damages. All benefits are subject to deductions for losses caused by a Member’s misdemeanor, with proof required by the Member to the satisfaction of the Vice President. Any overpayment, premature payment, or misdirected payment (an “Excess Payment”) must be restored promptly to the Plan. In exchange for receiving an Excess Payment, the recipient grants the Plan a constructive trust and first priority equitable lien on the Excess Payment or its proceeds, increased by appropriate interest, and the right to offset future payments from the Plan, at the Vice President’s discretion. The recipient also waives any rights to jurisdiction based on residence and submits to any court of competent jurisdiction for enforcement. The recipient must take all actions requested by the Vice President to recover the Excess Payment. This subsection maximizes the Plan’s rights to recover improper payments and does not restrict those rights. A Member forfeits their Pension if the Vice President determines they were terminated for cause or engaged in Prohibited Misconduct prior to the second anniversary of employment termination, and any previously paid Pension must be recovered. Prohibited Misconduct includes (1) accepting employment or ownership in a business that markets, sells, distributes, or produces “Covered Products” (such as beverages, juices, dairy, snacks, cereals, and value-added products) unless the business makes retail sales or consumes such products without competing with PepsiCo, (2) soliciting a PepsiCo employee to leave or join another entity, (3) using or disclosing confidential information (including customer, supplier, financial, operational, or strategic data) not necessary for their role, (4) engaging in acts contrary to PepsiCo’s best interests, including violating the Code of Conduct, unlawful trading based on insider information, or gross misconduct, and (5) engaging in fraud. Notwithstanding these provisions, Members may communicate with government authorities about possible legal violations without notice, participate in investigations, or receive awards for such disclosures, and the Corporation retains attorney-client privilege. Under the Defend Trade Secrets Act, individuals are not liable for disclosing trade secrets to government officials or attorneys for reporting suspected violations, or in sealed complaints, and may use such information in court proceedings if filed under seal and not disclosed except by court order. “Participation” includes serving as a director, officer, employee, consultant, or contractor, providing input, advice, guidance, or recommendations, or giving a testimonial on behalf of a business entity. “Covered Products” include any product in categories such as beverages, juices, dairy, snacks, cereals, and value-added food products, wherever PepsiCo produces, markets, sells, or licenses them.

The trade secret is kept under seal and is not disclosed except pursuant to a court order. For the purposes of this subsection, “Participation” is broadly defined to include serving as a director, officer, employee, consultant, or contractor with respect to a business entity; providing input, advice, guidance, or suggestions to such a business entity; or providing a recommendation or testimonial on behalf of such a business entity or one or more products it produces. “Covered Products” refers to any product that falls into one or more of the following categories—beverages (including carbonated soft drinks, tea, water, juice drinks, sports drinks, coffee drinks, energy drinks, and value-added dairy drinks), juices and juice products, dairy products, snacks (including salty snacks, sweet snacks, meat snacks, granola and cereal bars, and cookies), hot cereals, pancake mixes, value-added rice products, pancake syrups, value-added pasta products, ready-to-eat cereals, dry pasta products, or any product or service that the Member had reason to know was under development by the PepsiCo Organization during their employment with PepsiCo. Any notice required under the Plan to be given to or served upon the Plan is deemed sufficient if it is in writing and delivered to the Vice President. If notice is required to be given to Members, it is sufficient if delivered to the Member’s last known address on file or via any other method (e.g., electronically) that the Vice President determines is reasonably available to the Member. Every Member is entitled on demand to a copy of the governing legal document for the DB Program. Benefits under the Plan are paid in United States dollars or other “eligible currency” as approved by the Vice President, with amounts otherwise payable in U.S. dollars converted to the selected currency using an exchange rate based on a methodology approved by the Vice President from time to time. The Plan is governed by and interpreted according to the laws of the State of New York. The Plan is intended to be exempt from the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974, as amended (“ERISA”), as a plan maintained outside the United States primarily for the benefit of persons substantially all of whom are nonresident aliens of the United States. To preserve this exemption, both Active Membership in the Plan and the opportunity to increase Highest Average Monthly Earnings after ceasing to be an Active Member, as provided in Section 4.04(b), shall be limited to individuals who are nonresident aliens of the United States and whose assigned work locations are outside the United States, and all permanent records and documentation relating to the administration of the Plan shall be kept outside the United States. The Plan is also intended to be completely exempt from United States Internal Revenue Code section 409A (“Section 409A”), and shall be subject to the special operating rules and limitations in this Section 9.14, effective for any period to which Section 409A applies. It is intended that no Member who is a U.S. Person may have their benefit from the Plan vest, increase, or be enhanced (collectively, a “Benefit Enhancement”) as a result of their compensation or service while a U.S. Person. Therefore, no Member shall become entitled to a Benefit Enhancement with respect to a calendar year until it is determined, following the close of such year, that the Member was not a U.S. Person for such year. Notwithstanding, in the calendar year a Member’s benefit under the Plan is scheduled to commence, the Vice President may authorize a Benefit Enhancement for that year if they determine satisfactorily that the Member will not be a U.S. Person for such year. In all other cases, the Member’s benefit will commence without any Benefit Enhancement related to the calendar year of commencement, and appropriate adjustments will be made in the following year if it is determined that the Member was not a U.S. Person in that year. This Section 9.14 shall always be interpreted and applied in accordance with the overriding requirement that benefits and any other rights under the Plan must remain entirely exempt from Section 409A, and the Vice President shall have such unrestricted authority as necessary to ensure this requirement is met. Table A sets forth the formulas for calculating the Pension payable to a Member under Article IV or the Death Benefit payable to a Member’s Eligible Spouse or Eligible Domestic Partner under Article VI, subject to the freeze of the Plan described in Article I. Any benefits accrued by a Member while a part-time employee, following designation by the Vice President as an Eligible Employee under Section 2.01, shall be prorated as determined by the Vice President to reflect the approximate ratio of the Member’s level of services during part-time status to the level required for full-time status at their work location. (I) Member’s Pension: For Members who became members before January 1, 1976, the Pension payable at Normal Retirement Date as a Single Life Annuity is the larger of (1) 1.5 percent of the Member’s Highest Average Monthly Salary multiplied by the number of years of Pensionable Service, or (2) 3 percent of the Member’s Highest Average Monthly Salary multiplied by the number of years of Pensionable Service, not exceeding 15 years. For Members who became members on or after January 1, 1976, and for persons who became members on or after September 1, 1980 (excluding those in the first group), and for persons who became members after November 12, 1998 (excluding those in the first two groups), the Pension is calculated as the aggregate of (1) 3 percent of the Member’s Highest Average Monthly Salary multiplied by the number of years of Pensionable Service, not exceeding 10 years, plus (2) 1 percent of the Member’s Highest Average Monthly Salary multiplied by the number of years of Pensionable Service in excess of 10. At the discretion of the Vice President, the Pension may be reduced by: (1) all state pension and social security benefits attributable to service other than those from unmatched and unreimbursed voluntary contributions by the Member; (2) the annuity equivalent of a like portion of all capital sum benefits from retirement due to local legislation or termination indemnities; (3) benefits from other retirement plans or cash allowances of the Employers for periods qualifying as Pensionable Service under both the DB Program and such other plans; (4) any severance payments made at termination due to a severance agreement; (5) the value (as determined by methodology approved by the Vice President) of any benefits paid prior to retirement from any plan for periods qualifying as Pensionable Service under both the DB Program and such other plans; and (6) any deductions, reductions, or forfeitures due to misdemeanor, misconduct, or discharge for cause under Section 9.08. No such deduction applies to benefits from unmatched and unreimbursed voluntary contributions by the Member. The value of all such deductions is subject to adjustment for form and timing of payment, and all deductions are calculated as of the Member’s termination date using a methodology approved by the Vice President. If the Pension is reduced under paragraph (c), an alternative calculation applies unless the Vice President determines it is unnecessary or impractical or fails to serve the purposes of the DB Program. Under this alternative calculation, only the Member’s Pensionable Service under the DB Program (excluding employment considered in paragraphs (c)(1)–(5)) is considered, and reductions under (c)(1)–(5) are disregarded (though the reduction under (c)(6) is taken into account). The Pension under this alternative calculation is compared to the Pension under (a), (b), and (c), and the greater amount is payable, subject to the remaining provisions of this paragraph (d). This alternative calculation is intended to replicate the effect of the “extended wearaway” methodology as in effect under the PepsiCo Salaried Plan. Notwithstanding, any benefit increase resulting from this paragraph (d) will be limited by the Vice President to not exceed what should be available given the intent described. For purposes of this Table A, “Highest Average Monthly Salary” means one twelfth of the yearly average of the Member’s Salary over any 5 consecutive calendar years of Service in which such Salary was highest (or a lesser period if the Member has been in Service less than 5 years). In determining the Highest Average Monthly Salary, a calendar year with no Salary is disregarded, and the preceding and following years are considered consecutive. If a calendar year includes an unpaid authorized leave or other absence from paid service resulting in less than a complete year of Salary, that year is disregarded and the next preceding or succeeding year or years are taken into account if it results in a higher average. In determining the amount of a Deferred Vested Pension under Section 4.04, the Pension shall be equal to the greatest of the amounts determined under (1), (2), or (3): (1) the Pension calculated under (b) based on Pensionable Service the Member would have earned had they remained an Active Member until their Normal Retirement Age (subject to a maximum of 35 years) and Highest Average Monthly Salary as of September 30, 2003, reduced by a fraction with numerator equal to the Member’s actual years of Pensionable Service prior to October 1, 2003 (subject to a maximum of 35 years) and denominator equal to the years of Pensionable Service they would have earned had they remained an Active Member until Normal Retirement Age; (2) the aggregate of (i) the Pension calculated under (b) based on Pensionable Service the Member would have earned had they remained an Active Member until Normal Retirement Date and Highest Average Monthly Salary as of September 30, 2003, reduced by a fraction with numerator equal to the Member’s actual years of Pensionable Service prior to October 1, 2003 and denominator equal to the years of Pensionable Service they would have earned had they remained an Active Member until Normal Retirement Date; and (ii) the Pension calculated under (b) based on Pensionable Service the Member would have earned had they remained an Active Member until Normal Retirement Date and Highest Average Monthly Salary at the date the Member ceases to be in Service, reduced by a fraction with numerator equal to the Member’s actual years of Pensionable Service after September 30, 2003 and denominator equal to the years of Pensionable Service they would have earned had they remained an Active Member until Normal Retirement Date; (3) the Pension calculated under (b) based on Pensionable Service the Member would have earned had they remained an Active Member until Normal Retirement Date and Highest Average Monthly Salary at the date the Member ceases to be in Service, reduced by a fraction with numerator equal to the Member’s actual years of Pensionable Service and denominator equal to the years of Pensionable Service they would have earned had they remained an Active Member until Normal Retirement Date. Any Active Member who does not meet all of these requirements is not a Covered Employee and is not eligible for benefits under this Appendix ERW. The Reorganization refers to the reorganization, plant closing, or other event that triggered the applicable Severance Program. The Severance Date is an Active Member’s final day of employment with the Employer pursuant to the Reorganization. For the 2007/2008 Restructuring, the Severance Program includes both the “PepsiCo Transition Severance Program for the 2007 Restructuring for Salaried Employees Below Band 1” and the “PepsiCo Transition Severance Program for the Equipment & Service Management Restructuring for Salaried Employees below Band 1,” with an Effective Date of February 4, 2008.
